title: Module 7 check: point estimation and confidence intervals

questions.prompt: Why is the sample variance calculated by dividing by n − 1 rather than by n?
options: Dividing by n − 1 makes it unbiased: on average it equals σ², while dividing by n averages a little less
Dividing by n − 1 makes it efficient: it has a smaller variance than the estimator that divides by n
Dividing by n − 1 makes it resistant: one outlier cannot move it as far as it moves the n version
Dividing by n − 1 makes it match the population variance σ², which also divides by n − 1
questions.explanation: Deviations from x̄ are a little smaller than deviations from μ, so Σ(x − x̄)²/n averages (n − 1)/n × σ². Dividing by n − 1 removes that bias: E[S²] = σ². It is about bias, not efficiency or outliers.

questions.prompt: For a normal population, the sample mean and the sample median are both unbiased estimators of μ, and the median's variance is about 1.57 times the mean's. What does this say?
options: The mean is the more efficient estimator: from the same n it lands closer to μ, on average
The median is the more efficient estimator, because its larger variance covers more values
The median is biased, because its variance is larger than the mean's variance
The two are equally good, because both of them are unbiased estimators of μ
questions.explanation: With both unbiased, the one with the smaller variance is more efficient. The mean's estimates are more tightly grouped around μ; the median would need about 57 % more data to match it. A larger variance does not make an estimator biased.

questions.prompt: The daily water demand of households in a town has mean 320 L and standard deviation σ = 90 L, and is skewed to the right. A utility averages the demand of a random sample of **n = 81** households. What is the standard error of the sample mean, in liters? Give it to two decimals.
questions.explanation: σ/√n = 90 / √81 = 90 / 9 = 10.00 L. With n = 81, the central limit theorem makes the sample mean close to normal, mean 320 L and standard deviation 10 L, although single households' demand is skewed.

questions.prompt: Times between failures of a pump are strongly skewed to the right. An engineer has n = 60 of them and builds a t interval for the mean. Why is that reasonable?
options: By the central limit theorem the mean of 60 values is close to normal, even though single times are skewed
The central limit theorem makes the 60 failure times themselves normal once n is above 30
A t interval does not need the sample mean to have any particular distribution
It is not reasonable: an interval for a mean needs the data to be normal at every sample size
questions.explanation: The CLT is about the sample mean: for large n it is approximately normal, whatever the population's shape. The data keep their skew. With a small sample from a skewed population, the interval would not be reliable.

questions.prompt: Ten welds were pull-tested: x̄ = 12.4 kN, s = 1.5 kN. Find the **upper limit** of the 95 % confidence interval for the mean strength μ. (t_{0.025, 9} = 2.262.) Give it to two decimals.
questions.explanation: σ is unknown, so use t with n − 1 = 9 degrees of freedom. SE = 1.5 / √10 = 0.4743 kN; E = 2.262 × 0.4743 = 1.073 kN; the interval is 12.4 ± 1.073, from 11.33 to 13.47 kN. With z = 1.960 the upper limit would be 13.33, too narrow for ten welds.

questions.prompt: Twelve samples of a river's dissolved oxygen give x̄ = 7.8 mg/L and s = 0.6 mg/L. No earlier data on the river's σ exist. Which interval is right?
options: x̄ ± t_{α/2, 11} · s/√12, because σ is estimated by s
x̄ ± z_{α/2} · s/√12, because the river's oxygen is approximately normal
x̄ ± t_{α/2, 12} · s/√12, because there are twelve samples
x̄ ± t_{α/2, 11} · s, because each sample varies by s
questions.explanation: With s in place of σ, use t with n − 1 = 11 degrees of freedom, times the standard error s/√n. z needs a known σ; df is n − 1, not n; and s alone is the spread of single samples, not of x̄.

questions.prompt: Of 200 randomly chosen intersections in a county, 36 have a crash rate above the state's threshold. What is the **margin of error** of the 95 % confidence interval for the proportion of all the county's intersections above the threshold? (z_{0.025} = 1.960.) Give it to three decimals or more.
An engineer's 95 % interval for a mean is too wide to be useful. She can afford **four times** as many measurements as she took. If s stays about the same, what happens to the margin of error?
options: It is about halved, because the standard error falls with √n and √4 = 2
It falls to about a quarter, because the standard error falls with n
It stays about the same, because s and the confidence level do not change
It doubles, because more measurements bring in more of the variability
questions.explanation: E = t·s/√n. Four times n doubles √n, so E is about halved (a little less than half, since t also falls slightly as the degrees of freedom grow). To cut E to a quarter would take sixteen times the data.

questions.prompt: A transit agency wants to estimate the proportion of riders who pay with a phone, within **±0.04** at **95 %** confidence. It has no earlier estimate of the proportion. How many riders must it survey? (z_{0.025} = 1.960.) Give a whole number.
questions.explanation: With no earlier estimate use p = 0.5: n = (1.960 / 0.04)² × 0.5 × 0.5 = 2401 × 0.25 = 600.25. Always round up: 601 riders. Rounding to 600 would leave the margin just over 0.04.

questions.prompt: A 95 % confidence interval for the mean service life of a bridge bearing type is 41.5 to 47.0 years. Which statement interprets it correctly?
options: We are 95 % confident that the mean life of this bearing type is between 41.5 and 47.0 years: 95 % of intervals made this way contain the true mean
There is a 95 % probability that the mean life of this bearing type is between 41.5 and 47.0 years, now that the interval is calculated
95 % of bearings of this type will last between 41.5 and 47.0 years, so a bearing can be planned to last 41.5 years
The mean life of this bearing type is 44.25 years, the center of the interval, with an error of 5 % at most
questions.explanation: The confidence describes the method's long-run success rate; the calculated interval either contains μ or not. The interval is for the mean, not single bearings, which vary much more. And the center is only the estimate x̄.
